narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your LSAT score, your undergraduate GPA, and your academic performance in the third year of law school. Your LSAT score of 21.3 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure; it is far below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted. Your third-year class ranking was the next most important factor and also increased the chance of failure. While accepted students typically rank around the 5.8 decile in their third year, you ranked in the 2nd decile, a noticeable drop from your first-year performance which matched the accepted-student average.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure, but its positive effect was not large enough to offset the other two factors. Your family income, full-time status, gender, and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and strengthening your academic performance in later law school years. Retaking the exam with a significantly higher score would be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
